news.title: Elon Musk’s net worth surges by $61bn as SpaceX and Tesla shares rally toward trillion-dollar milestone
news.text:
Elon Musk’s net worth increased by $61 billion on Friday, reaching $979.7 billion and pushing his fortune back toward the $1 trillion mark.

The surge was driven by strong market rallies across his key enterprises, with SpaceX shares rising over 7% following a series of successful launches and Tesla stock climbing roughly 5% after beating third-quarter delivery expectations.

Musk maintains a commanding lead on the Forbes Real-Time Billionaires list, sitting $600.5 billion ahead of second-place Jeff Bezos, whose net worth stands at $370.7 billion.

Billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk experienced a massive financial rebound on Friday, adding $61 billion to his fortune in a single day as shares in both SpaceX and Tesla rallied significantly. 

According to the Forbes Real-Time Billionaires list, Musk’s estimated net worth climbed to $979.7 billion, representing a 6.64% increase from Thursday and bringing him within striking distance of reclaiming a permanent trillion-dollar valuation.

The surge was anchored by strong operational and market momentum across Musk’s corporate portfolio. SpaceX shares advanced over 7% to trade at $158.84 following an intensive 24-hour window of successful missions, including human spaceflight deployments to the International Space Station and experimental orbital artificial intelligence tests. 

Simultaneously, Tesla stock gained around 5% to trade at $371.32 after the electric vehicle manufacturer announced robust third-quarter deliveries totaling 486,532 vehicles. The delivery figures comfortably surpassed analyst projections, bolstering investor sentiment and alleviating concerns over consecutive annual declines.

Musk continues to dominate the global wealth rankings, holding the No. 1 spot comfortably ahead of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, who occupies second place with an estimated net worth of $370.7 billion. Market analysts note that while Musk previously crossed the $1 trillion threshold following SpaceX’s public debut earlier in the year, subsequent market volatility has caused his net worth to fluctuate around the milestone.

Managing extreme equity volatility in high-valuation technology and aerospace ventures creates rapid fluctuations in executive net worth metrics.

Aligning production milestones and quarterly delivery targets remains vital for sustaining investor confidence in high-growth electric vehicle and space infrastructure markets.

WHAT’S BEING SAID

“Elon Musk’s net worth was at $979.7 billion as of 2:15 p.m. on Friday, a 6.64% hike from Thursday, according to the Forbes Real-Time Billionaires list.” – Forbes Real-Time Billionaires List

WHAT’S NEXT

Market observers will monitor upcoming quarterly earnings reports and further launch schedules for SpaceX and Tesla to determine whether Musk’s fortune will permanently surpass the $1 trillion mark.

BOTTOM LINE

Elon Musk’s net worth jumped by $61 billion on Friday to $979.7 billion, fueled by a powerful stock rally across SpaceX and Tesla that brought the world’s richest individual back to the doorstep of a trillion-dollar fortune.

news.title: New Zealand electric car registrations triple as petrol tops $3 a litre
news.text:
Electric car registrations in New Zealand roughly tripled in the three months to the end of September, as petrol at well over $3 a litre pushed households and businesses toward cars that cost less to run.

The number of electric vehicles registered in the September quarter was up 206 percent on a year earlier, RNZ reported on Friday from figures analysed by Infometrics. Full battery electric registrations rose 230 percent and plug-in hybrids 169 percent. Conventional hybrids, which cannot be plugged in, rose a much more modest 7.7 percent.

Battery electric cars and plug-in hybrids made up 19 percent of all car registrations in the quarter, up from 7 percent a year earlier. Infometrics counted 55,317 passenger car registrations over the three months, up 14 percent year-on-year and above 50,000 for the first time since the end of 2023.

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen tied the shift directly to the pump. The price of 91 octane climbed through the quarter from a low of $2.90 a litre to $3.35 by the end of September.

“I think what we’re seeing at the moment is that there’s quite a big focus from both households and businesses on trying to get the most fuel efficient and cost-effective option,” Olsen told RNZ. “Even if they’ve got to pay a bit more upfront for a new EV, it’s still got better running costs over time.”

He said petrol and diesel registrations were continuing to fall as buyers made “a much stronger decision on what car they might be purchasing next.”

“Funnily enough New Zealand consumers are fairly rational,” he said. “When prices go high for fuel people think ‘maybe I’m better off looking at an EV’ and they have.”

That is a sharp turnaround from the slump that followed the end of the clean car discount. Electric and plug-in hybrid sales fell away heavily after the government scrapped the rebate at the end of 2023, and only began to recover this year. Olsen said some observers had wondered whether the early 2026 spike in interest would fade once the first wave of buyers had been through.

“We were wondering, was this sort of just a quick flash in the pan?” he said. “We’re now sort of six months in, and you have seen things continue.”

His explanation is that buyers no longer expect relief at the pump. Households and firms weighing up a vehicle were concluding that “fuel prices do remain high. I don’t necessarily think they’re going to become cheap any time soon,” he said. A wider choice of electric models at different price points was also helping.

Monthly figures released earlier in the week point the same way. New vehicle registrations reached 17,055 in September, up 21.8 percent on September 2025, according to Autotalk’s analysis of NZ Transport Agency data. New passenger registrations rose 27.8 percent to 13,244, although rental fleets did a fair share of the lifting. Rental companies took 4736 of the month’s new passenger cars, or 35.8 percent, and accounted for 41 percent of the year-on-year increase.

Toyota stayed comfortably on top with 3003 passenger registrations, and the Toyota Corolla Cross was the best-selling passenger model with 1053. But the fastest movers were electric brands. BYD registered 871 new passenger vehicles in September, up 714 percent on a year earlier, and Tesla registered 650, up from 228, with the Tesla Model Y the fifth best-selling passenger model on 588. Tesla tends to bunch its deliveries at the end of each quarter, so its monthly numbers jump around.

Counting its commercial models as well, BYD said it registered 1090 vehicles in September, the first time it has passed 1000 in a month in New Zealand, AutoTrader reported. The Chinese company, which entered the New Zealand market in 2022, said its Atto 2 was its best seller for the month, and it has just added a plug-in hybrid version of that car priced from $34,990.

“This represents real buyers choosing lower running costs, better technology and strong value, not a number built on subsidies or fleet deals,” BYD Auto NZ general manager Warren Willmot said.

Six Chinese brands between them took 20.3 percent of the new passenger market in September, up from about a tenth a year earlier. A month ago Chinese brands had taken almost a fifth of August registrations, so their share is holding rather than spiking.

For the wider economy the shift matters in two ways. Every car that runs on New Zealand electricity rather than imported petrol trims the national fuel bill, at a time when the country is paying more for oil and has little buffer if supply is disrupted. It also changes the second-hand market a few years out. Rental and new-car fleets bought now become the used cars of 2028 and 2029, which is how ordinary buyers who never purchase new eventually get access to cheaper electric motoring.

There are limits to the trend. Electric and plug-in cars are still fewer than one in five registrations, and New Zealand’s existing fleet of several million cars, vans and utes turns over slowly. Petrol and diesel cars will make up most of what is on the road for years yet, which is why pump prices remain one of the biggest pressures on household budgets. Readers can follow how those prices are moving week to week on our New Zealand fuel price tracker.

Whether the surge lasts will depend largely on oil. If petrol eases back below $3 a litre the case for paying more up front for an electric car weakens. If it stays where it is, Olsen’s view is that buyers will keep doing the sums and keep reaching the same answer.

Have petrol prices changed what you would buy for your next car, or have you already made the switch? Tell us how the numbers stacked up for you in the comments below.

news.title: Honda Super-One has a lot of attitude
news.text:
Freo fans took over Melbourne ahead of last Saturday’s AFL grand final —and Honda’s Super-One electric car was out in, err, purple, buzzing around city streets to show the motoring media pack exactly what this cheeky little runabout can do.

Hells Bells! It was looking like a dead cert for the Dockers on the day — but they triggered Wharfie Time too soon, with the Brisbane Lions scoring four goals in the final minutes to win by seven points.

Heartbreaking.

And yeah, looks like Kylie pocketed $3 million for her 20-minute pre-game gig.

The Super-One is Honda’s first EV in Australia and looks best in purple — which Honda calls Boost Violet Pearl — though you can get Crystal Black and Luminous Grey, as well, plus two-tone Boost Violet Pearl with Crystal Black roof — if you’re prepared to wait.

By all accounts, it sold out as soon as order books opened in August, with the initial allocation of 130 cars snapped up within hours. First deliveries were due to start on October 1.

More are on the way as Honda Australia targets 500 sales over the next 12 months, acknowledging it is a niche market, with the Super-One’s quirky design based on Japan’s kei car concept — though it’s not a kei car.

What’s a kei car?

Kei is short for short for kei-jidosha, a class of ultra-compact cars unique to the Japanese domestic market, with strict conditions on body size and engine outputs. They must be less than 3396mm long (the Super-One is 3582mm), 1475mm wide (the Super-One is 1573mm) and 2000mm tall (the Super-One is 1616mm). Engines can’t exceed 0.66 litres (petrol and hybrid), with a maximum power output of 47kW.

They account for half the country’s sales thanks to tax benefits, cheaper insurance, and parking exemptions in many rural areas.

Honda’s N-Box has been the top-selling kei car in Japan for several years.

Drive-away pricing

Forget about specs. There are two Super-One grades based on colour combo.

+ Mono — Crystal Black, Luminous Grey or Boost Violet Pearl: $36,900

+ Two-tone: Boost Violet Pearl with Crystal Black roof: $37,400

What’s it like?

It’s a five-door hatch with four seats and weighs in at just 1093kg — which makes it about 310kg lighter than similarly sized cars.

Of course, little cars have big ideas, so this one features Honda’s signature “magic seats” at the rear that fold flat and flip up to maximise storage with 18 configurations — and more cargo capacity than an SUV with seven passengers: 967 litres with the second row down, loaded to the roof (otherwise it’s 162L).

Front sports seats look good in two-tone fabric and leather, but I find the cushion bolsters make them feel a bit narrow through the hips and thighs.

Exterior styling draws inspiration from the 1980s Honda City Turbo II, with sustainability in mind. Notably, Honda has collected, smashed and recycled bumpers from its discarded cars to use in the front end.

There are also various recycled materials inside, a leather-wrapped steering wheel with blue stitching, buttons for temperature and air flow, a lovely eight-speaker Bose sound system, a 9.0-inch touchscreen that’s easy to navigate, plus a 7.0-inch instrument cluster, both wired and wireless Apple CarPlay and wireless Android Auto, Google Built-in.

It also has a three-year subscription to Honda Connect Gen 2 that has digital key functionality via a smartphone, automatic collision detection and lets you check things like battery status, schedule charging or set a geofence alert.

It starts from the back rooftop carpark — renamed Izakaya Honda for the day — in Federation Square.

We do 26km in just over an hour split between two drivers, most of it at snail’s pace in peak-hour CBD streets, driving straight through Chinatown and alleys cluttered with bins, past Orica House (formerly the ICI building), and along the outskirts of Melbourne’s historic brothel district “Little Lon” because this is pitched as a city car, after all. I also manage to get in a 100km/h run coming back into town.

Luckily, there are no hook turns, a Melbourne idiosyncracy that takes a right from the left lane to stop cars from blocking trams that travel down the middle of the road.

The Super-One has a single motor producing 47kW and 162Nm as standard to drive the front wheels using a (nominal) 29.6kWh lithium-ion battery.

Range is 202km WLTP.

There are five drive modes — Eco, Normal, Sport, City and Boost — which is a lot for a little car. Flick it into Sport, and it growls obnoxiously, which is all sound effects through the speakers, so no one thinks you’re a hoon.

The Boost button is on the steering wheel and increases peak output to 70kW, with a rev counter and fake gear shifts as the instrument cluster turns from blue to purple.

Oh, there’s a G-force meter, as well.

Really, Boost is the only way to travel on highways, and makes you appreciate how agile and responsive the car is.

City mode is fine crawling through traffic, and lets you engage one-pedal driving, making it possible to largely stay off the brake.

Specs list only the turning radius: 5.2m. This is not the same as the turning circle, which works out at 10.4m — and that’s more than I would expect from a little nipper.

Claimed energy consumption is 12.1kWh/100km, but various people have taken out the ones on test here and we come back with 145km range on an 85 per cent charge and energy consumption averaging 18.2kWh/100km — which is high for something this size on 15-inch wheels when a Tesla Model 3 RWD on 18-inch wheels uses 12-14kWh/100km in mixed driving.

What this means for real-world driving, I’m not sure, given it’s generally not encouraged to charge a lithium-ion battery to 100 per cent all the time. I guess if you’re prepared to keep it topped up to, say, 80 per cent, it will do the job as a city car.

Plugging into a standard 10-amp socket overnight should be enough, otherwise the onboard charger — technically an AC to DC power converter — has a maximum charging capacity of 10kW. Typically, you’d be looking at around four hours to charge from 15 per cent to 100 per cent using a 6.6kW single-phase wallbox, or about three hours with a 10kW three-phase set-up.

Otherwise, Honda estimates a 50kW DC charger will take about 30 minutes to get from 15 to 80 per cent.

Is it safe?

The Super-One has not been crash tested by ANCAP or Euro NCAP.

It comes with six airbags, front and rear parking sensors, a reversing camera and Honda Sensing active safety that includes, among other things, forward-collision warning, traffic-jam assist, adaptive cruise control, post-collision braking, lane-departure warning and a lane-keep assist system (activated by pressing a button on the steering wheel).

Warranty and servicing

The Super-One has a five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty; five years of premium roadside assistance; and five years of capped-price servicing costing $199 each time. The warranty and roadside assist can be extended by three years if the car has been serviced by Honda. Servicing is every 12 months/15,000km, and the high-voltage battery comes with an eight-year/160,000km warranty.
news.summary: It’s the automaker’s first electric vehicle in Australia

news.title: Rivian’s sales pop as the company’s big R2 bet starts to pay off
news.text:
Rivian had high hopes for its more affordable R2 vehicle — and so far, those hopes appear to be paying off.
The company released its third-quarter production and delivery numbers today, reporting 19,751 vehicles produced and 19,248 delivered. That represents an 85 percent year-over-year increase in production and a 45 percent jump in deliveries. (For a direct-to-consumer automaker like Rivian, deliveries serve as a proxy for sales.) The company also reaffirmed its full-year 2026 guidance, expecting to deliver 65,000 to 70,000 vehicles.
Rivian’s sales surge is a rare bright spot in a struggling industry. A year after President Trump and Republicans in Congress eliminated the $7,500 federal EV tax credit, broader EV sales have predictably plunged. According to Cox Automotive, as of September 2026, overall EV sales were down nearly 24 percent year-over-year. Tesla just reported a 2.1 percent decrease in Q3 sales (though that was better than expected).
Rivian has been telling investors it will sell upwards of 25,000 R2s in its first year of production, which would make it one of the fastest launches of a new electric vehicle in US history. The R2 needed to be a hit for Rivian to survive as an independent company. As Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe told us earlier this year: “R2 is the most important thing we have because it’s what takes us from being subscale to being a scaled manufacturer.”
While Rivian doesn’t break down sales by model, the company expects full-year deliveries for both its R1 lineup—the R1T truck and R1S SUV—and its electric delivery van to remain flat. Last year, Rivian delivered over 13,000 vehicles in the third quarter. Assuming R1 and van deliveries held steady, that leaves approximately 6,000 R2 vehicles delivered to customers this quarter.
The sales report comes amid a string of good news for Rivian. The company recently announced that the R2 hit its climate goal of reducing its lifetime emissions by 50 percent four years ahead of schedule.

news.title: Tesla sustains its EV sales momentum despite US troubles
news.text:
Tesla sold more than 480,000 EVs in the third quarter, as the company continues finding ways to move new cars despite its troubles in the U.S. market. 

It was the second strong quarter in a row for Tesla after a somewhat rough start to the year. The sales figure easily beat out consensus estimates from Wall Street and topped even the most optimistic view for the company, which made its 10 millionth vehicle earlier this year. 

The company said Friday morning that it built 464,391 vehicles in the quarter and delivered more than 486,532. That’s an increase of roughly 6,000 vehicle deliveries compared to the second quarter. But sales were still down from the same period last year, when Tesla delivered 497,000 vehicles. That quarter — Tesla’s best ever — was helped by a rush of U.S. buyers who were looking to take advantage of an expiring federal tax credit.

Before Friday’s numbers were released, Tesla’s sales were down nearly 20% year-over-year in the U.S. market, according to Cox Automotive.

That drop has been the result of a number of factors. Tesla has not released any new consumer models in years — with the exception of the Cybertruck, which has been a commercial flop. Potential buyers have also balked because of Elon Musk’s personal support of Donald Trump’s presidential campaign and his role overseeing the Department of Government Efficiency, which laid off thousands of workers and canceled international aid funding.

Tesla has looked to other markets to make up for lost U.S. sales. The company’s sales are on the rise again in Europe, where EVs are more widely adopted and supported by tighter emissions regulations. Tesla is reportedly expanding capacity at its factory in Germany to meet that demand. The company has also seen continued strong sales out of its factory in China despite competition in the region, with some of those sales driven by Tesla looking to newer markets like Japan, Australia, and Lithuania.

Despite the rebound in overall momentum, sales have become something of a taboo subject for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who is increasingly focused on the company’s other efforts. Perhaps the biggest example is the Cybercab, which Tesla started putting on the roads of Austin, Texas in recent weeks. The two-seater EV has been giving autonomous rides to passengers despite having no driver, steering wheel, or pedals.

Tesla also recently launched the production version of its electric big rig, nearly a decade after it was first introduced. The company aims to make roughly 50,000 Tesla Semi vehicles per year.

Other new efforts are in the works, but don’t have firm commercial timelines. The second-generation Roadster is set to be re-revealed on October 15 after years of delays, though it’s not clear when it will get built. Tesla is also developing the Optimus humanoid robot, but has repeatedly pushed back its timeline. Earlier this week, Tesla announced it had secured up to $30 billion in new lines of credit to support these projects.
news.summary: The company delivered more than 486,000 EVs in the third quarter, down from last year's record but moving in a positive direction.
news.author: Sean O'Kane

news.title: Stock Market Today, Oct. 2: Tesla Rises on Q3 Delivery Beat
news.text:
Tesla (TSLA +4.65%), a global electric vehicles (EV), battery storage, and energy software provider, closed at $370.59, up 4.65%. Tesla rose after reporting Q3 deliveries that beat Wall Street estimates, and investors are watching October earnings and energy-storage trends next.

Trading volume reached 53.9 million shares, coming in about 39% above its three-month average of 38.7 million shares. Tesla IPO'd in 2010 and has grown 23,208% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.73%) closed at 7,723, up 0.74%, while the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.19%) finished at 27,191, up 1.19%. Among electric vehicle and energy storage manufacturing peers, Rivian Automotive (RIVN -3.12%) closed at $14.30, down 3.12%, and Lucid Group (LCID -1.43%) closed at $4.13, down 1.43%.

What this means for investors

While Tesla's competitors experienced share price declines, the EV leader continues to prove why it's the preeminent electric carmaker. On Friday, Tesla's third-quarter deliveries of 486,532 topped consensus estimates by about 25,000 vehicles, reinforcing the company's near-term demand momentum. This result is particularly impressive, considering federal EV tax credits expired in September of 2025.

Of the 486,532 vehicle deliveries, Tesla's Model 3 and Y comprised 478,237 of them. These low-cost models remain popular with consumers, with the Model Y achieving three consecutive years as the world's best-selling car as of the end of 2025.

Wall Street is now watching whether the electric automaker's production and delivery strength carries into results and guidance. The better-than-expected deliveries suggest Q3 sales could be excellent. Tesla's $28.2 billion in Q2 revenue represented outstanding 26% year-over-year growth.

On the same day, rival Rivian announced it had accomplished a record high in Q3 deliveries and reaffirmed full-year guidance. This is significant, since it points to fresh marketwide EV demand, suggesting Tesla's delivery beat could be part of a stronger industry recovery. 

Tesla has experienced a busy year. The company officially launched its autonomous-vehicle Cybercab in September, a robotaxi service that will compete with ride-hailing businesses, such as Uber, and began deliveries of its semi trucks, marking another product milestone.
news.summary: Tesla's Q3 deliveries of 486,532 vehicles topped consensus estimates by roughly 25,000 units, signaling sustained demand momentum, today, Oct. 2, 2026.
news.author: Robert Izquierdo

news.title: Stock Market Today, Oct. 2: Rivian Beats Q3 Delivery Estimates on Record Production Pace
news.text:
Rivian Automotive (RIVN -3.12%), the maker of electric pickup trucks, SUVs, and commercial delivery vans closed at $14.30, down 3.12%. Shares spiked at the open after the positive Q3 delivery news was announced. Still, investors later focused on the unchanged full-year outlook and are watching for Rivian's Oct. 29 full financial results.Trading volume reached 59.1 million shares, coming in about 107% above its three-month average of 28.6 million shares. Rivian Automotive IPO'd in 2021 and has fallen 86% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.73%) closed at 7,723, up 0.74%, and the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.19%) finished at 27,191, up 1.19%. Among electric vehicle (EV) manufacturers of automobiles and light trucks, Tesla closed at $370.59, up 4.65%, while Lucid Group closed at $4.13, down 1.43%, highlighting a mixed session for EV names.

What this means for investors

Friday's delivery update revealed 19,248 vehicles delivered and 19,751 produced. Those were strong numbers, but still in line with company expectations. It led Rivian to reaffirm its 2026 delivery outlook. That was underwhelming for investors, and Rivian stock gave back all the early gain and more.

To meet the full-year vehicle delivery guidance, the company will need to report over 28,000 units shipped in Q4 to reach the high end of the range. That's what investors are waiting to see.

The Q3 results represented a 46% increase over the same period last year. Yet the company's estimates for this year suggest it could nearly triple fourth-quarter deliveries from last year.

If Rivian achieves that, it would confirm growth and momentum, and that may be when investors will decide to move shares higher.
news.summary: Rivian's record Q3 delivery beat lifted shares early before investors refocused on unchanged guidance and the Oct. 29 earnings call, today, Oct. 2, 2026.
news.author: Howard Smith

news.title: Tesla Delivered 486,532 Vehicles in Q3. Here’s Why the Real Test Could Come on Oct. 21.
news.text:
Shares of Tesla (TSLA +5.05%) had surged roughly 4.8% as of 12:44 p.m. ET on Oct. 2, after the electric vehicle maker reported higher-than-expected third-quarter deliveries.

Tesla said it delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter, with production of 464,391. Deliveries are the closest measure Tesla provides for vehicles sold, while production is the number of vehicles built at Tesla's factories in a given quarter.

Wall Street analysts had only expected Tesla to deliver 461,100 vehicles, so it was a big beat on consensus.

Deliveries rose about 1.3% from the prior quarter, although they were still down about 2% year over year. Production rose about 2.8% from the prior quarter.

Tesla also said it deployed 13.7 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy storage capacity through its commercial and residential battery-storage systems. The company deployed 13.5 GWh last quarter.

While the delivery beat is encouraging, as evidenced by the market's reaction, the real test will come on Oct. 21, when Tesla reports its full third-quarter earnings and holds a conference call with analysts.

EVs are no longer part of the core business moving forward

While Tesla helped commercialize electric vehicles in the U.S. and still accounts for the bulk of its revenue, the business is no longer part of Tesla's investment thesis.

To put things into perspective, Tesla in 2025 generated total revenue of nearly $95 billion and $1.08 diluted earnings per share. The company currently trades at nearly a $1.5 trillion market cap, so it's tough to say that the EV business is driving the stock.

Furthermore, part of the better-than-expected deliveries in the third quarter can be attributed to an improvement in the broader EV market.

As oil prices have surged due to the Iran war, that's created a better proposition for EVs. The renewables sector could see increased investment in the coming years, due to national security concerns exposed by the Iran war.

It's all about robotaxis and humanoid robots

As most people who follow Tesla now, the future of the business and stock at this valuation is fully self-driving (FSD) robotaxis and humanoid robots, which the market believes Tesla holds a big advantage in.

Tesla has already launched its robotaxi fleet in seven markets: Austin, San Francisco, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, and Tampa. Tesla also recently launched the Cybercab, a two-seated vehicle with no steering wheel, manual brakes, or side mirrors.

Still, it doesn't seem like Tesla has achieved fully unsupervised FSD yet, or at least it hasn't fully rolled it out in its robotaxi fleet. Most of the new markets are geofenced and involve some level of remote monitoring.

Meanwhile, Tesla's Optimus humanoid robots, which will supposedly be able to perform household chores and which Tesla CEO Elon Musk believes will be the company's "biggest product ever," have not yet been rolled out.

Limited manufacturing of Optimus has begun, but it could be a long process before it reaches wide-scale production because the company essentially has to build a supply chain for robots from scratch.

So, while the improvement in the EV business is certainly good news, I don't think it's a long-term driver of the stock. 

What will be more important on Oct. 21 is when Musk and the rest of Tesla's management team provide an update on robotaxis and Optimus.

Given the stock's valuation, I think investors should wait for more evidence that both robotaxis and Optimus can scale effectively before buying. 

The timeline for these products seems to be constantly changing, and there’s still no guarantee that each will work as effectively or be as successful as the market currently believes.

Investors have grown impatient. Tesla stock has underperformed the broader market over the past five years and is down roughly 15% this year.
news.summary: Tesla's third-quarter deliveries soundly beat Wall Street consensus estimates.
news.author: Bram Berkowitz

news.title: Stock Market Midday, Oct. 2: Stocks Rally as Weak Jobs Data Cools Fed Rate Hike Bets
news.text:
As of 11:38 AM ET, the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.21%) is up 1.18% to 27,191, hitting a record high as soft labor data boosted tech stocks. The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.70%) has climbed 0.70% to 7,720, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +0.37%) is trading 0.35% higher to 51,107.

Gold is trading at $4,141.21, down 0.90%, as the 10-Year Treasury yield rises 2 basis points to 5.25%. Most sectors were in the green, with industrials and consumer cyclicals leading the gainers, while energy and financial services stocks lagged. 

Today's biggest moves

Tesla is surging more than 5% today after reporting better-than-expected vehicle deliveries. ON Semiconductor and Synaptics are surging after announcing a revised merger agreement. Integra LifeSciences is tumbling after lowering its financial guidance.

What this means for investors

Stocks are rising today as investors process a September jobs report that shows an unexpected slowdown: The U.S. added 29,000 jobs last month, and unemployment rose to 4.2%. It may seem counterintuitive for markets to gain on signs of a cooling economy, but the data makes it less likely that the Federal Reserve will raise rates this month, and that is good for riskier assets. Traders now put the likelihood of an October rate hike at 21%, down from 64% last week.

Several semiconductor leaders, including Nvidia (NVDA +2.29%), set new all-time highs alongside the Nasdaq. Artificial intelligence (AI) enthusiasm is building again, particularly as investors eye the upcoming Anthropic IPO and the high demand for infrastructure. Nvidia's $150 billion in share buybacks only adds to confidence that the AI boom will continue.
news.summary: Today, Oct. 2, 2026, September employment came in cooler than expected, spurring a broad market advance and renewed optimism among growth investors.
news.author: Emma Newbery
